content: To improve adherence to treatment, it is essential to provide tailored support, including options for home-based or community-based follow-up. Early identification and tracing of individuals who miss appointments should be implemented to ensure continuity of care. The use of fixed-dose combination medications is recommended to enhance adherence. For example, the fixed-dose combination tablet containing co-trimoxazole, pyridoxine, and isoniazid, as utilized in the REALITY trial, has been recently added to the WHO List of Essential Medicines. The package of interventions for individuals with advanced HIV disease, as outlined in the 2016 WHO consolidated ARV guidelines, should be offered universally to all patients presenting with advanced HIV disease. Detailed recommendations are provided in Annex 1 of the guidelines. For diagnostic purposes, sputum Xpert® MTB/RIF should be the first test for tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis in symptomatic individuals. Lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) testing is recommended for TB diagnosis in individuals with CD4 cell counts ≤100 cells/mm³ or in those who are seriously ill, regardless of CD4 count. Cryptococcal antigen screening is advised for individuals with CD4 counts ≤100 cells/mm³. Prophylactic and pre-emptive treatments include co-trimoxazole prophylaxis for individuals with CD4 counts ≤350 cells/mm³ or those in clinical stages 3 or 4, as well as TB preventive treatment and fluconazole pre-emptive therapy for cryptococcal antigen-positive individuals without evidence of meningitis. Rapid initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) is recommended, except in cases where clinical symptoms suggest TB or cryptococcal meningitis, to avoid life-threatening immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). Adherence support should be tailored to individual needs, including counseling and, where feasible, home visits for individuals with CD4 counts <200 cells/mm³. Fixed-dose combination tablets containing co-trimoxazole, isoniazid, and pyridoxine are available to simplify treatment regimens and improve adherence. Presumptive treatment for TB, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, bacterial infections, and cryptococcal disease should be considered in settings with limited access to diagnostic tests, particularly for individuals presenting with typical signs and symptoms of these conditions. The WHO algorithm for managing individuals with HIV who are suspected of having TB and are seriously ill incorporates presumptive treatment into the care pathway. Medications such as co-trimoxazole, TB preventive treatment, and fluconazole pre-emptive therapy should be initiated as soon as the criteria for intervention are met. ART initiation should be deferred in cases of suspected TB or cryptococcal meningitis to prevent paradoxical worsening of the infection. Providing a package of essential interventions focuses on diagnosing, preventing, and treating the most common causes of morbidity and mortality among individuals with advanced HIV disease. However, attention should also be given to other severe illnesses not covered by the package, particularly in regions with high prevalence of specific comorbidities and coinfections. The increased pill burden and potential side effects may impact adherence, but in clinical trials, fixed-dose combination tablets were well-tolerated and considered easy to take by most participants. The cost of implementing the package of care may be offset by savings from reduced hospitalizations and treatment of opportunistic infections. Equity and acceptability considerations highlight the importance of addressing the needs of vulnerable groups, such as men, who are more likely to present with advanced HIV disease and have higher associated mortality rates. Community consultations have shown support for providing a package of interventions to reduce mortality and morbidity in advanced HIV disease. Feasibility challenges include the additional costs of the package, training of healthcare workers, and ensuring sufficient human resources to provide intensive adherence support. Baseline CD4 cell count testing and the cost of additional medications may also pose challenges in resource-limited settings. Implementation of the package of care requires adapting current service delivery models, particularly in resource-limited settings. Decentralized care and mobile outreach can improve access, supported by point-of-care diagnostic tests or sample transport systems. Clear referral criteria and communication mechanisms are essential to ensure timely access to specialist care and appropriate follow-up. For individuals with advanced HIV disease, rapid ART initiation should be offered unless clinical symptoms suggest TB or cryptococcal meningitis. Presumptive treatment should be initiated in seriously ill patients if diagnostic results are unavailable or delayed. Treatment literacy strategies and community-based support are critical to improving adherence and identifying signs of advanced HIV disease. The package of care should be available at both hospitals and decentralized primary care clinics, depending on the clinical status of the patient, the skills of healthcare workers, and access to diagnostics. Referral mechanisms and communication following discharge must be optimized to ensure continuity of care. Where referrals are not feasible, advice from experienced clinicians and presumptive treatment at peripheral sites should be considered.
